newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Bank of England needs wider focus - analysts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bank of England needs wider focus - analysts.

text.p: The Bank of England is over-zealous in its quest to hit the government's inflation target and is neglecting the overall needs of the British economy, a growing band of independent economists say.
Despite a patchy economic recovery and huge uncertainty over the pace of future growth, the Bank insists interest rates need to rise by a quarter-point.
And it has dismissed the pound's spirited rally since last summer as temporary and unlikely to have far-reaching effects.
"The heart of the problem is the Bank has been a little too literal in interpreting its remit on inflation," said Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Europe.

"When we are embarking on a year in which everyone believes inflation is going to fall and when there are so many uncertainties, not least the full implications of sterling's rally, why press for a rate rise?"

The Bank, which advises the Chancellor on monetary policy, has been charged with hitting a tough 2.5 percent target for underlying inflation over the medium term and wants to see an immediate rate rise to improve its chances of succeeding.
Inflation, at 3.1 percent in January, is stuck some way above the target, but it has fallen to its lowest level in 30 years despite five years of expansion.
However, the economic recovery is badly out of kilter, combining a struggling manufacturing base barely out of recession and a service sector fast approaching a boom.
The Bank believes the fast growing services sector, and lively consumer spending in particular, pose a threat to inflation so rates should rise.
Some economists believe an interest rate rise now would only serve to magnify the imbalance by punishing manufacturers and pushing prices of exports up even further.
"Higher rates now could actually make the imbalance even worse if it pushed the pound higher," said Briscoe.
But it is the Bank's blase attitude to sterling's upward march that has left it particularly vulnerable to criticism.

Always quick to point out the inflationary risks when the pound depreciates, the Bank said in its November inflation report tht the rally since August, then about nine percent on a trade-weighted basis, would not last and had no implications for inflation in the medium term.

Three months on in its February report, when the pound had gained a further seven percent, the Bank said the pound's continued strength would only result in a one-off fall in inflation in the short term.
"The Bank has been too sniffy on the on effect sterling is having and underplaying the effects of a strong exchange rate," said Geoffrey Dicks, UK economist at NatWest Markets.

David Philpotts, economist at Schroders, agreed the Bank has gone too far in dismissing the full impact of sterling's stellar performance. "It has played down the second round effects of the pound's rally. It is quite likely lower import prices mean wage pressures will take longer to pick up."
But Philpotts said the Bank is right to point out sterling's rally does not address the biggest threat risk to sustained low inflation -- strong domestic demand.
"Domestic demand is not going to go away because lower import prices are washing through the system. The Bank wants to address the cause of the danger not the symptom."
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has ignored calls for higher rates from Bank Governor Eddie George at their last three monetary meetings.

But while the Bank is accused of getting it wrong on rates, economists say that in terms of the inflation target, neither has Clarke got it right. "We have not got inflation down to the original target -- 2.5 percent by the end of the Parliament -- so collectively they have got it wrong," Dicks said.
